summary: Specifies a Mobility Header message that a home agent can send to a mobile node to say it should switch to a new home agent. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: If the helper looking after your phone's mobile address needs to be swapped, this is the message that tells the phone to move to a new helper.

questions: what is the home agent switch message
how does a mobile node switch home agents
subtitle: A signal that tells a Mobile IPv6 node its home agent is going away and where to look for a new one.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) has no way for a home agent to tell a mobile node that it must stop serving it, for example because the home agent is overloaded or going offline.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Mobility Header message, the Home Agent Switch message (MH Type 12), that lists alternate home agent addresses. The mobile node answers by deleting its home binding and picking a new home agent.
tldr.outcome: Operators can move mobile nodes between home agents in a controlled way, provided they limit the rate of messages so the new home agent is not swamped.

today: RFC 5142 is a Proposed Standard from January 2008. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem and Scope
sections.content:
In Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) a home agent keeps a binding for each mobile node, but the base protocol has no provision for a home agent to tell a mobile node that it must stop acting as its home agent. A home agent might want to hand off nodes because it has become overloaded or is going offline.

RFC 5142 defines one signaling message for this, the Home Agent Switch message. It deliberately does not solve everything. It does not cover the case where the mobile node's Home Address must change to switch home agents (that operation should be avoided using this message), and it does not decide when a home agent should move nodes. That decision is left to a backend protocol, for example the Home Agent Reliability Protocol work cited as a work in progress.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone has a helper that forwards its mail. Until now the helper had no polite way to say 'I have to stop, go find someone else'. This message is that way.

sections.title: Scenarios for Switching
sections.content:
The RFC lists five example situations where such a message helps:

  • Overloaded: the home agent is at or near its limit on home bindings, or has reached a set level of memory or CPU use, and wants to shed bindings before a failure occurs.
  • Load balancing: the home agent knows of less loaded home agents (learned by some other mechanism) and an operator wants a failure to disrupt a smaller percentage of mobile nodes.
  • Maintenance: a home agent about to be shut down can warn nodes so they do not lose mobility service.
  • Functional load balancing: one set of home agents handles the rendezvous function and another handles tunneling. A node found to be reverse-tunneling instead of doing route optimization can be redirected to a home agent with better data throughput.
  • Renumbering: a provider moves home agent service to a new set of IPv6 addresses and tells nodes to look for a new home agent.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper might be too busy, need a day off, be told to move offices, or just be better at one job than another. In all those cases the helper wants to hand you over to a friend.

sections.title: The Home Agent Switch Message
sections.content:
The message uses the Mobility Header format from Section 6.1 of RFC 3775 with the MH Type value 12. Its Message Data field holds:

  • Number of Addresses: an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the number of IPv6 home agent addresses in the message. If it is zero, the mobile node MUST perform home agent discovery.
  • Reserved: 8 bits, set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.
  • Home Agent Addresses: the list of alternate home agent addresses.
  • Mobility Options: zero or more TLV-encoded options, padded so the whole Mobility Header is a multiple of 8 octets. A receiver MUST ignore and skip options it does not understand. The Binding Refresh Advice option from RFC 3775 is valid here.

If no addresses and no options are present, no padding is needed and the Header Len field is set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The note says how many other helpers to try, then lists their names in order. If it lists none, you have to go look for a helper yourself.

sections.title: What the Home Agent Does
sections.content:
The sender builds an ordinary Mobility Header with MH Type 12. If it knows alternate home agents it SHOULD list them, built as in Section 10.5.1 of RFC 3775, which randomizes addresses of equal preference. It MUST fill in the address count field and sets it to zero when no addresses are given. If it can keep serving the node for a while, it MAY add a Binding Refresh Advice option giving the time (in units of 4 seconds) until the binding will be deleted. A home agent SHOULD send the message ahead of a known period of unavailability.

The sender need not be the node's current home agent, but it MUST have a security association with the mobile node. In that case the message SHOULD contain only the sender's own address, which implies the node should switch to the sender.

Retransmission. If no Binding Update arrives in reply, the home agent SHOULD retransmit, starting at INITIAL-HA-SWITCH-TIMEOUT and doubling the timeout each time until it reaches MAX-HA-SWITCH-TIMEOUT. It MAY keep sending at that slower rate indefinitely. If a Binding Refresh Advice option was included, it SHOULD delay retransmissions until half that period has passed or the initial timeout, whichever is less.

Errors. A node that cannot process the message sends a Binding Error. A node that stays unreachable should not be assumed to be anything in particular, and the home agent SHOULD keep serving until the binding lifetime expires. Further Binding Updates that try to extend the lifetime SHOULD be rejected with status value 129 (Administratively prohibited).
sections.plainLanguage: The helper says 'please go' and repeats it, waiting twice as long between tries, until you answer. While you are leaving, the helper keeps working but will not renew your contract.

sections.title: What the Mobile Node Does
sections.content:
On receipt, the node first verifies the Mobility Header as RFC 3775 requires and checks that the packet was covered by the home agent to mobile node IPsec ESP authentication SA. Failures follow Section 9.2 of that RFC, for example a Binding Error with Status 2 (unrecognized MH Type value) if the type is unsupported.

The node MUST then stop using its current home agent and MUST delete its home binding with a Binding Update. That Binding Update acts as the acknowledgement. If the sender was not the current home agent, a Binding Update that creates a home binding acts as the acknowledgement instead. With a Binding Refresh Advice option, the node MAY keep using the old home agent until the stated time has passed.

If addresses were listed, the node SHOULD pick one and set up IPsec security associations with it. If none were listed, it MUST first perform home agent discovery.

Choosing. Usually the addresses belong to home agents on the home link (same computed prefix), and the node SHOULD try them in listed order. If prefixes differ, the node SHOULD prefer addresses with its own home network prefix first. A different prefix might force a home address change and break connections using the old address.
sections.plainLanguage: When you get the note, you check it is really from your helper, tell the helper 'ok, I am leaving', and then try the new helpers on the list one after another, starting with the first.

sections.title: Operational Limits
sections.content:
The RFC does not say how operators should use the message but sets requirements. Because a home agent may serve thousands, if not millions, of mobile nodes, careless use may overload the new home agent or other parts of the network. It is REQUIRED that deployments either use a feedback loop between the new home agent's resources and further messages, or apply a maximum rate far below the capacity for new registrations. Without other information the default is MAX-HA-SWITCH-TRANSMIT-RATE.

Switching should happen only when absolutely necessary, because the new home agent may fail or be overloaded, and path characteristics may change and trouble end-to-end transport. For load balancing, all home agents in the set should be configured with the same prefixes so no home address change is needed. Changing the address is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: If a thousand kids are all sent to the same new helper at once, the new helper gets swamped. So only send a few at a time, and only when you really must.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
As with other RFC 3775 messages, the Home Agent Switch message MUST use the home agent to mobile node ESP encryption SA for confidentiality protection and MUST use the home agent to mobile node ESP authentication SA for integrity protection. It MAY reuse the ESP SA already in place for Binding Updates and Acknowledgements, to cut the number of configured security associations. Some operators may not want to reveal the list of home agents to on-path listeners, which is the reason to use the encryption SA.

IANA assigned Mobility Header type 12 to the Home Agent Switch message.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is sealed and signed so nobody can fake it or read the list of helpers on the way.
